tier_reason: The CHANGES file's 0.8 entry (lines 1083-1086) states 'Benchmark on 1000 random ints: glibc: 679414 cycles qsort and 3352 cycles bsearch / diet libc: 300010 cycles qsort, 553 cycles bsearch', matching the record; it is a first-party changelog line with no benchmark code in the repo, no compiler, flags, CPU model or glibc version, so C.

corrections.workload: qsort and bsearch on 1000 random ints, measured in CPU cycles, as recorded in the dietlibc 0.8 changelog entry (2001 or earlier; lib/qsort.c history in the mirror starts 2001-02-11). The qsort that was measured has since been replaced twice (new qsort 2003-11-02, 'faster qsort' 2006-08-16, random pivot via rand_i 2019-01-29).
corrections.caveats: First-party, one changelog line from the 0.8 release (2001 or earlier) with no benchmark program, compiler, flags, CPU model or glibc version stated; the author adds 'I have no idea why glibc is so slow.' The measured qsort no longer exists: lib/qsort.c was rewritten on 2003-11-02 ('write new qsort that does not fail so'), again on 2006-08-16 ('faster qsort', the 0.31 'faster qsort' changelog line) and given a random pivot on 2019-01-29, so the 2.3x figure describes code that is gone. The current qsort is a recursive Sedgewick 3-way quicksort with a byte-by-byte swap loop, no insertion-sort cutoff and no recursion-depth bound; glibc's qsort has also changed many times since 2001. Independent counter-evidence (snippet only, nullprogram.com 2016 'Inspecting C's qsort Through Animation', page EGRESS_BLOCKED): glibc's qsort finished the animated sort in 307 frames versus 503 for dietlibc 0.32, and the author calls dietlibc 'optimized for size, which shows through its slower performance'. The bsearch gap (3352 vs 553 cycles for a single lookup in 1000 ints, about 10 comparisons) is far larger than two plain binary searches can differ algorithmically; it probably reflects first-call costs such as lazy PLT binding of a dynamically linked glibc or cold caches, which the changelog does not control for. Size is dietlibc's real selling point and is not benchmarked in the repo. The FAQ says dietlibc can 'improve performance by an order of magnitude for certain programming models' and points to fefe.de/fnord/SPEED; fefe.de was EGRESS_BLOCKED here. The same changelog notes an i386 strlen that is '31% faster, 14% smaller', but its baseline is the older dietlibc C version, not glibc. repo_url is the unofficial ensc git-cvs mirror, archived 2023-09-05 with its last commit on 2019-03-18; upstream lives in CVS at cvs.fefe.de and may be newer (the mirror's CHANGES already has an unreleased 0.35 section). License is GPL-2.0 'or later' per README, so linking it into distributed binaries carries GPL obligations.

notes: Numbers are on the page exactly as recorded and the baseline (glibc qsort/bsearch) is named, so the entry stands at tier C, but the claim is a 25-year-old one-liner about a qsort implementation that has since been replaced twice, and a 2016 independent animation (snippet only) shows dietlibc 0.32's qsort doing more work than glibc's; record it as 'probably not faster today, measured code gone, no methodology'. maintenance_status corrected to abandoned (mirror archived 2023-09-05, last commit 2019-03-18). Not a duplicate of any listed project.
